prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B015, Katori and Ye) as a single-part prize. After the first round the case rests on one point that the chair rightly asks us to settle: is this distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize? My answer is yes, and it is an experimental answer. A comb is a ruler for optical frequency, and an ion clock interrogates one trapped particle, which limits its statistical stability. The magic-wavelength condition removes the differential light shift of the trap, so that many thousands of neutral atoms can be probed at once, Doppler- and recoil-free, in a single coherent measurement. That is what moved stability by orders of magnitude and made 1e-18 systematic evaluation feasible in reasonable averaging times. The evidence that settles it is that independent lattice clocks (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, and several national laboratories) are intercompared at the 1e-18 level, and that these clocks resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres and probe many-body effects inside the clock itself, which no earlier tool could do. For the citation division the chair asks about, I would anchor it on the lattice scheme and its realization: Katori for the concept and the first strontium lattice clocks, and Ye for taking the same scheme to the accuracy and stability frontier. I would leave the redefinition of the second out of the citation. It is supporting evidence that the field is mature, not a condition for recognition, and a prize should not wait on a metrological procedure. Eight of eight members ranked it and all eight name the same two people, and I do not see another entry on this list that combines that agreement with experimental reproducibility.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged but sharper after reading Danielsson and Eriksson: a skeptic can say that this is a superb instrument and not yet a finding about nature, since the clock-based searches for dark matter and varying constants have so far produced only tighter bounds. That is a real difference from IceCube, which delivered an unforeseen observed flux, and if the committee weights discovery over capability I understand why B007 or B006 would come first. A second reservation is attribution at the edges: PTB, NIST, SYRTE, Tokyo and others contributed cold-atom engineering, ultrastable lasers and systematic evaluations, and Ye's many-body clock results are a later extension, so the wording must not suggest a single origin of the clock family. Finally, I recall the priority details of the lattice proposals from memory and have not verified them here.

responses.point: Danielsson asks what nature told us in B015 that we did not know, and holds that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is not fully answered; he ranks IceCube first but accepts B015 as the safer choice with a cleaner attribution.
responses.response: Ulf, I take the 'what did nature tell us' question seriously, and my honest answer is that it told us how well nature can be measured: a quantum system with 10^-18 systematics reproduced on several continents, and a gravitational redshift visible across a millimetre, which is a measured fact and not an inference. The discovery content in dark matter and constants is still null bounds, and I do not claim otherwise. On overlap I have tried to answer concretely above: the magic-wavelength condition is what allows many neutral atoms to be used at once, which neither the comb nor ion control provided. On B007 I have tested my own view against your argument. My round-1 question about a Halzen and Karle pair is still open, and with Olsson on two names, Pearce and you on three, and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage, I do not think the credit is settled this year. So I keep IceCube as my first alternative and would not oppose it in a later year, but I would not trade a settled two-name prize for an unsettled three-name one. Can you accept B015 if the citation is worded around the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 performance, which is your 'what does it add' test?

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene for its quantitative prediction followed by decisive experiment, concedes B015 is clearly ahead on robustness, and says he would accept B015 if the committee prefers it, though he wants us to test what it adds beyond 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: Olle, I accept your test and have tried to meet it: the added element is the magic-wavelength trap and what it enabled, a new regime of stability and a many-body clock, not a better comb or a better ion. On B006 I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is the clearest theory-to-experiment chain we have, and I now rank it higher than I did in round 1, which is why it appears among my alternatives. My remaining concern is experimental: the superconducting phase differs between devices, twist-angle inhomogeneity is large, and Yuan Cao and the groups of Dean, Young, Efetov and Yazdani are outside three names. Mehlig's proposal to anchor the citation on the flat band and the correlated insulators would handle the mechanism problem, but not the credit problem. I would therefore regard B006 as a strong later prize, not an obstacle to B015 now.

responses.point: Olsson separates Katori's invention and early strontium clocks from Ye's later record accuracy, accepts the pairing because Ye's group proved the 1e-18 operating regime, and wants the citation to name the lattice scheme and not just precision.
responses.response: Eva, I agree with both of your conditions and have worded my citation accordingly: it names magic-wavelength trapping and the realization, and the 10^-18 level is the consequence and not the claim. You asked in round 1 whether Ye's role is the original invention or a later realization. I think it is the second, in the sense that the invention is Katori's, but the realization the committee should credit is the demonstration that the scheme works as a clock at the accuracy frontier, and Ye's group did a large part of that with the strontium clocks and their systematic evaluation. I would not describe that as later work only. I also note that your first choice B013 and my B057 have both fallen back for the same reason, a narrow base of support and an unresolved credit question (Krivanek and Dellby for B013, Chu and Borde for B057), so I do not think B013 can become a second part of a prize this year.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved to B015 because of the shape of the committee's evidence, asks that the citation rest on invention and performance, and challenged my second alternative B057 as having a more entangled credit than Katori and Ye.
responses.response: Mark, I accept that challenge and it changes my alternatives. I ranked atom interferometry second because it is a new measurement capability in the same spirit, but the credit among Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich, and the uncredited Chu and Borde, with Chu's part partly covered in 1997, is not something I can defend in three names, and no other member has found a clean allocation either. I therefore drop B057 from my alternatives. The two-part configuration, B015 paired with a measurement-driven discovery, was my own round-1 suggestion, and I have tested it: the only sensible partner is B007, and Katori, Ye plus Halzen, Karle and Spiering is five people, above the three-person limit, so it would force a two-name IceCube that only Olsson proposes. That is not a better prize than one clean prize. Where I still differ slightly from you is that I would not rest the case on agreement alone, since agreement among eight members on names is a weaker argument than the reproducibility of the clocks themselves.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers twisted bilayer graphene as a simple, understood mechanism followed by experiment, and argues that waiting for the pairing mechanism does not ease attribution; his alternatives are B055 and B015.
responses.response: Bernhard, your argument that the prize would honour the flat-band mechanism and the discovery of correlated states, not a theory of pairing, is the best form of the B006 case, and I agree that waiting for the mechanism does not fix the credit question, so I do not treat the superconductivity as disqualifying. Where I still differ is on the experimental evidence: the correlated insulators and the superconducting dome are reported in devices with strong sample dependence, and a citation of experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states invites questions about which groups first reproduced which phase. I would ask whether you would accept B015 with the citation we have discussed, since you list it among your alternatives and describe the lattice clock as a clean original idea followed by a precision realization.

uncertainties: The exact priority of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal relative to closely related lattice proposals, and how much realization credit belongs to Ye's group versus PTB, NIST and RIKEN, rest on my memory of the literature and have not been verified here.

Whether the committee will accept the distinctness argument against the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or will still see lattice clocks as a capability prize in an already honoured line; I regard it as distinct, but Danielsson and Eriksson are not fully persuaded.

Whether recognising an instrument and capability, with only null results in dark-matter and constants searches so far, is what the prize should do this year, compared with an unforeseen discovery such as IceCube.
The size of the many-body clock contribution to Ye's credit, which I consider real but not essential to the core claim.
statement.conflict_note: No direct collaboration, institutional tie or financial link to Katori or Ye is apparent. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory at JILA during my PhD, and Jun Ye is at JILA, so there is a shared lineage and community but no joint work; I judge that this does not require recusal, I disclose it for the record, and I would accept the committee's view if others disagree. My quantum sensing role in the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, with its institutional link to Chalmers and member Johansson, bears on B024 and B010, and I would recuse from those. My company interest, Deep Light Vision, concerns ultrasound optical tomography and not timekeeping, so it has no bearing on B015.
